summary.text: Ovid's fifteen-book song of changed forms — from Chaos and the ages of man through divine loves, mortal pride, and the punishments of heaven, until Caesar rises among the stars: a Roman tapestry woven from Greek myth, where nothing keeps its shape for long.

chapters.title: The song of change
chapters.text: The poet opens with a promise to tell of bodies changed to new forms from the beginning of the world to his own day — and asks the gods to breathe upon his undertaking, for they themselves wrought the changes he must sing.

chapters.title: Gods and mortals alike
chapters.text: Through flood and famine, through rape and revenge, through contest and hubris, Ovid returns again and again to the same device: the body altered — laurel, spider, stone, bird, star — so that desire, pride, or pity may be fixed forever in a new shape.

chapters.title: The Roman frame
chapters.text: The catalogue is not merely Greek antiquity retold: the poem closes with Julius Caesar's apotheosis and Augustus' reign, so that metamorphosis becomes the lens through which Rome too reads its own succession of power.
